title: Atoms & the periodic table
why: Everything downstream is built from three facts: how many bonds an atom makes, how electronegative it is, and how many valence electrons it has. Get these automatic and the rest of the week is pattern-matching instead of memorizing.
how: Read the Notes first — including the orbital refresher and the element table. Then run two Study sessions, and finish with a Speed round.

title: Lewis structures & formal charge
why: Formal charge is the single most under-practiced skill going into orgo, and it shows up in every mechanism from week one. If you can't spot a charged atom instantly, arrow-pushing never clicks.
how: Use the interactive builder questions — set the bonds and lone pairs and watch the charges appear. Then Study, then the spot-the-error questions, which are the closest thing here to an exam question.

title: Polarity & molecular shape
why: Polarity tells you WHERE a molecule reacts (the δ+ carbon is what gets attacked). VSEPR tells you what it looks like in three dimensions. Together they turn a flat drawing into something with reactive sites.
how: Bond Polarity first — it is a direct application of yesterday's electronegativity. Then VSEPR Notes, then the diagram-based shape questions.

title: Skeletal structure fluency
why: This is pure repetition and the highest-value day of the week. Orgo is written almost entirely in line-angle drawings; if reading them takes conscious effort, you will burn your attention on notation instead of chemistry.
how: Speed rounds, repeatedly. Aim to read implicit hydrogens without counting. Then Study for the harder formula and unsaturation questions.

title: Functional groups & intermolecular forces
why: Functional groups are the vocabulary of the whole course — every reaction you will learn is named for what it does to one. Intermolecular forces then explain why those groups change boiling point and solubility, which is what lab work turns on.
how: Functional Groups first, with a Speed round for recognition. Then IMF Notes and Study — the boiling-point comparisons are the core skill.

title: Acids & bases
why: Almost every orgo mechanism opens or closes with a proton transfer, and pKa is how you predict which way it goes. This is the day that pays off most once class starts.
how: Read the Notes for the pKa ladder, then Study. Focus on proton-transfer direction questions rather than raw pKa recall — reasoning beats memorizing here.

title: The bridge into orgo
why: Naming, resonance and arrow notation are where gen chem ends and organic chemistry actually begins. You do not need mastery before day one of class — you need to have seen them so lecture is a second exposure, not a first.
how: One Study session each, unhurried. Read every explanation. Then finish with Mixed Review to see how the week holds together.
